crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: AI and authorship concerns the question of who counts as an author when generative models or other AI systems contribute to research, writing, or data analysis. It covers human accountability for AI-generated text, the criteria for listing contributors, and the disclosure of AI assistance in scholarly work. The topic sits within research integrity because authorship signals responsibility for the work, and AI involvement can blur that signal. It also includes the distinction between using AI as a tool and treating it as a co-author, which most current norms reject.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The practical setting includes manuscript preparation systems, preprint servers, journal submission portals, and collaborative writing platforms where AI assistance may be embedded. Authors may use large language models through chat interfaces, coding assistants, or integrated writing tools, and these systems often leave metadata or logs that can support provenance checks. Institutional repositories and version control systems also form part of the infrastructure, because they can record who changed what and when. The site's library of research papers and extracted claims provides a reference base for studying how authorship norms are described in published work.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work in this area is done by reviewing journal policies, analysing disclosure statements, and comparing author contribution records against detected AI-generated text. Researchers may use text classifiers, stylometric tools, or provenance logs to identify passages that lack clear human attribution. The method also includes qualitative analysis of retraction notices and ethics cases where AI use was undisclosed or misattributed. Because the site links to original papers rather than a search tool, readers can trace claims back to the source text and check the authorship context directly.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on accountability, plagiarism, and the integrity of the scholarly record. If an AI system drafts text, the named human authors remain responsible for its accuracy and originality, but undisclosed AI use can create ghost authorship and obscure who did the intellectual work. Provenance is therefore a key concern, with journals increasingly requiring statements about AI use and some publishers refusing to list AI tools as authors. Risk also includes copyright uncertainty over AI-generated passages and the possibility that generated text reproduces unattributed material.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more granular and machine-readable records of contribution, so that reviewers and readers can see exactly where AI was used. Publishers and funders are likely to converge on common disclosure standards, and institutions may adopt automated checks that flag undeclared AI assistance without replacing human judgement. Authorship itself may shift from a single byline to a structured set of roles and responsibilities, with AI use recorded as a tool rather than a contributor. The site's growing catalogue of papers, claims, and models will support comparative study of how these norms evolve across disciplines.
